entries.title: Google Launches LiteRT Tensor API for Building, Customizing, and Optimizing ML Models for On-Device
entries.summary: Google has introduced the LiteRT Tensor API, a lightweight C++ API that allows developers to build, customize, and optimize machine learning models directly for on-device execution. According to Google, it combines the flexibility of native model authoring with cross-platform portability. By Sergio De Simone
entries.content:
Google has introduced the LiteRT Tensor API, a lightweight C++ API that allows developers to build, customize, and optimize machine learning models directly for on-device execution. According to Google, it combines the flexibility of native model authoring with cross-platform portability.

The traditional approach, Google says, is for developers to write computations manually in C++ for maximum control, which comes with a significant drawback:

Implementations are tightly coupled to specific backends (such as Metal, OpenCL, or Vulkan) and must be rewritten for each new hardware target. Furthermore, managing zero-copy buffer interoperability and synchronization across CPU, GPU, and NPU, while gluing together pre-processing, inference, and post-processing, demands substantial manual engineering effort.

The LiteRT Tensor API aims to address these challenges by allowing developers to build computation graphs operation by operation in C++. This provided greater control over model architecture, optimization, and accelerator execution, while enabling the same graphs to run through LiteRT on CPU, GPU, and NPU hardware without requiring a rewrite for each new target.

Beyond providing full control over model graphs, other key capabilities of the API include direct weight ingestion, allowing developers to load weights directly from checkpoints, including Hugging Face 

.safetensors
files; zero-copy buffer interoperability, which avoids copying accelerator buffers across pre-processing, inference, and post-processing; and compatibility with AI coding agents, which can construct, modify, validate, and benchmark model graphs by generating C++ code.

Google used a coding agent to create a real-world app demonstrating how to use the LiteRT Tensor API for multi-object segmentation and tracking. The application also served as the basis for benchmarking performance across platforms:

We ran the same C++ code for the SAM 2 model on the GPUs of three devices: a macOS laptop (Metal), an iOS phone (Metal), and an Android phone (OpenCL). In our tests on the MacBook Pro, it ran about 1.5x faster than Apple MLX (fp16, image encoder plus mask decoder).

Google emphasized the fact that the coding agent could make a number of optimizations thanks to the model graph being defined in plain C++. Specifically, it "moved SAM 2's per-frame decisions, such as whether the object is still visible, from CPU code into the graph" and rewrote operations that triggered CPU fallback on WebGPU using GPU-compatible arithmetics.

Commenting on the announcement on LinkedIn, Arm director of AI Laurence Moroney emphasized that developers should always start with model conversion and turn to the C++ API only "when you need graph-level control or want pre and post-processing to stay on the accelerator". He also highlighted the benefits of defining model graphs in plain C++:

Going from under 10 to over 30 frames per second at 512x512 on WebGPU, with a coding agent doing the iteration, shows how much structured primitives help agents do real optimization work.

Google is also working on several planned improvmeents, including direct ML Drift backend support, additional NPU-friendly operations, automatic full-graph quantization, and expanded dynamic-shape for different image sizes, batch sizes, and sequence lengths.

entries.title: Vitest 5: Prioritises Performance with a Shared Vite Server, Trace View, and Stricter Test Defaults
entries.summary: Vitest 5.0 focuses on speed, with reported gains of 8 to 25 percent in most setups and up to 53 percent in VM pools. It adds a vitest doctor command, Browser Mode Trace View, and vi.when. Defaults are stricter: clearMocks is true and unawaited async assertions fail. It requires Vite 6.4 and Node.js 22.12 or newer. By Daniel Curtis
entries.content:
Vitest, the Vite-native testing framework maintained by VoidZero, has released Vitest 5.0, a major version that puts raw speed ahead of new surface area while quietly tightening several long-standing defaults.

Using a purpose-built benchmark suite that spans everything from a five-file utility package to a 1,280-module monolith, the team reports gains of roughly 8 to 25 percent across most setups, rising to 53 percent in VM pool scenarios. VoidZero summarised the release on X as "vm pools up to 53% faster, ~18% boost across the board including Browser Mode". The wins come from inline projects sharing a single Vite server, a stabilised on-disk 

fsModuleCache
, fewer round trips between the main process and workers, and VM pools that reuse compiled code. A new 
vitest doctor
command reruns a suite under alternative configurations and recommends faster options.

Browser Mode also gains a built-in Trace View that records each interaction and assertion as a DOM snapshot for step-by-step replay, while the new 

vi.when
API lets a single spy return different values per argument.

clearMocks
now defaults to true, unawaited async assertions fail rather than warn, hoisted 
vi.mock
calls placed outside the top level now throw, and 
toThrow('')
matches any error. As the independent OpenReplay breakdown puts it, most of these changes simply "break test code that was already wrong", but the dangerous ones are suites that pass locally on Vitest 4 and "go red in CI with an error that says nothing about why", usually call-count assertions that relied on mock history leaking between tests.

Vitest 5 requires Vite 6.4 and Node.js 22.12 or newer, and Yarn users must now install 

vite
themselves because it became a peer dependency. The migration guide and v5.0.0 changelog document each change, and reporter output, attachments, and blob reports now live under one 
.vitest/
directory, so CI artifact paths need updating. Ecosystem catch-up is ongoing: Cloudflare's vitest-pool-workers issue notes its peer range pinned to v4 means any project pulling the new release "fails before a single test runs".

Against Jest, a recent head-to-head comparison scores Vitest ahead on performance and future-proofing yet behind on ecosystem and community, reflecting Jest's far larger install base and first-class React Native support. The advice to anyone considering the choice is unchanged, reach for Vitest on Vite, Nuxt, or greenfield projects, leave large working Jest suites in place, and let the two coexist in a monorepo.

Vitest is an open-source, Vite-powered test runner developed by VoidZero, the company founded by Vite creator Evan You that has joined Cloudflare. It reuses a project's existing Vite configuration to run unit, component, and browser tests with native ESM and TypeScript support, and is backed by more than 790 contributors.

entries.title: LinkedIn Uses OpenTelemetry to Trace the Member Journey from Tap to Backend
entries.summary: LinkedIn has built an OpenTelemetry-based telemetry platform that connects what members do in its iOS, Android, and web applications with the backend services processing those interactions. By Craig Risi
entries.content:
LinkedIn has built an OpenTelemetry-based telemetry platform that connects what members do in its iOS, Android, and web applications with the backend services processing those interactions.

The goal is to close a common observability gap. Client analytics can show that a member tapped a button or encountered an error, while backend tracing explains what happened inside the services handling the request. Historically, connecting these views required engineers to correlate separate systems. LinkedIn's approach allows a member interaction to be followed from the client through frontend and backend services to the underlying data stores.

A single page can generate numerous requests, each potentially passing through multiple services. LinkedIn introduced a pageForestId to provide context above individual distributed traces.

Each request retains its OpenTelemetry traceId, while related requests from the same page context can be associated through the pageForestId. Engineers can therefore investigate both an individual request and the wider activity that contributed to a member's experience.

This is important because conventional distributed tracing generally follows one request, whereas a member journey can involve many related requests.

LinkedIn operates a diverse technology stack spanning mobile and web clients alongside backend services written in Java, Python, Go, and Rust. OpenTelemetry provides a common model for instrumentation, trace context, and semantic conventions across those environments.

LinkedIn has built its own wrappers and extensions around the standard OpenTelemetry SDKs, allowing product teams to use consistent instrumentation while the platform handles concerns such as mobile lifecycle, export, and LinkedIn-specific metadata.

Client and backend applications generate OpenTelemetry spans, with trace context propagated as requests move through the system. Shared HTTP and gRPC frameworks automatically instrument common request paths, while teams can add explicit spans around important business operations.

Telemetry is transported through Apache Kafka and stored in ClickHouse, with pageForestId, traceId, and timestamps providing the keys for correlation. This allows engineers to begin with a member-facing interaction and drill into the backend execution responsible for it.

Capturing every span would generate an enormous amount of telemetry, making sampling fundamental to the architecture.

LinkedIn uses coordinated head sampling so related client and server activity receives a consistent sampling decision. A pseudonymised member identifier helps maintain that consistency across the journey, preventing the client from being sampled while the corresponding backend trace is discarded, or vice versa.

The company also distinguishes valuable quality-of-experience telemetry from lower-value debugging information. LinkedIn estimates that up to 90% of some backend tracing volume could potentially be treated as debug-level data.

Client-side observability introduces additional constraints. Mobile applications can be suspended or terminated before telemetry is transmitted, so LinkedIn batches spans but can flush telemetry when an application moves into the background.

The platform also applies controls around what data can enter traces, including attribute allowlists, denylists, and redaction. This is important because distributed traces can otherwise become an unintended channel for sensitive application or member information

Traditional distributed tracing tools such as Jaeger and Grafana Tempo are primarily focused on following requests across backend services. Commercial platforms such as Datadog and New Relic also combine distributed tracing with real-user and application monitoring.

LinkedIn's approach is less about introducing a capability that these platforms cannot provide and more about making OpenTelemetry the common foundation connecting its client and backend telemetry. Its own pageForestId model adds a higher-level grouping around standard traces, while Kafka and ClickHouse provide a customised ingestion and storage architecture.

This also gives LinkedIn greater control over its observability stack and avoids making application instrumentation dependent on a particular commercial backend.

A member does not experience a traceId; they experience a page that loads slowly, an action that fails, or a feature that behaves unexpectedly. Connecting those experiences to the distributed systems behind them gives engineers a much more direct path from user impact to technical cause.

Entropy is going to continue to be there. That's just part of law of thermodynamics. Regardless of what we do, there's always going to be entropy.

When it comes to architecture, we're always managing entropy. That's going to be part of whatever we build. Even today without machine agents or in the past without machine agents, these were things that we would run into. Recovery, so maybe there is an issue in production or issue with some tests and whatever, and agents not able to recover from that. These are different types of agentic issues. Sometimes we don't really know the root cause. I do want to say while, for instance, models will continue to improve and the harnesses provided by our coding agent providers, they might focus more on the top and be able to bridge the gap between what they provide and what we're able to do today. However, the things on the bottom, like they're always going to be there. They always have been there even without machine agents. Just want to share that these types of failures, we're not here to control and prevent.

Instead, the alternative model is, how do we make ourselves resilient? Like the DevOps model, if something's going to fail and has failed, try to make it happen more often so that you have a much more resilient system so you know how to recover from those failures. Then, finally, another industry learning also comes from Birgitta, and she was sharing that a lot of the work today up to now has been more on the coding tasks related stuff and maintainability of code and things like that. What's a gap right now is behavioral stuff. Like, what about the product standpoint? What are those behavioral, functional requirements? How do we work with our coding agents to support those?

How?

That's what I'm going to talk about actually in this next section, because we've been doing this. We have been working on functional requirements. Right now, our focus is on all the non-functional requirements. How do we now apply functional requirements to the coding agent world? Where I would like to start, this is actually coming from 2020, this is coming from my architecture experience earlier. I looked back at this, remember I said it feels very deja vu-ish, to like say, this is the product engineering operating model that we used at edX. Can this now be applied here where we're thinking about agents? I'm working with some life science clients right now, and we're trying to put together an operating model as we're working with agentic code and stuff like that. I looked back at this to see how might we do this. Then, whatever canvas we might develop for the agents, how might we leverage from here?

Let's take this one by one of what we're talking about. You'll see overall, even then, we were thinking about, and this is just the human world, the define phase, the build phase, and review phase. As a product organization, when we're defining, we're thinking about what's the overall strategy, product strategy, what are the opportunities, what are those hypotheses that we might want to test and experiment with. We might do things like Lean Value Trees. We might do some opportunity mapping and so forth. Then the output of that could be things like the opportunity trees, the strategy documents, and so forth. Then when we're building and we're iterating, continuous iteration, lean startup type of style, we might experiment as we do this, so continuous discovery as we're building. Then there, those outputs are specifications as well as any other compliance reports and things like that that we generate from our CI/CD pipelines and so forth.

That was always something that we also did. Then there's the review aspect. This part is interesting. I did want to call it out. I don't think the visual does it justice. There is a time aspect to reviews. Then there's the people or the who aspect to reviews as well. Who is doing which reviews, and then when? Because not everything needs to happen all the time. There's microfeedback loops as well as macrofeedback loops. Then the team themselves would do reviews of their builds and do that in their own sprint demos and so forth. Maybe with their stakeholders and the customers. Then there might be some opportunity reviews that we might do with the product leader or the product organization that requested the change in the first place. Then there might be some strategic reviews. Those strategic reviews are not just with the business organization, but also the engineering leaders. Your VP of engineering, your CTO, whatnot, may want to be able to see, we said that we want to have these metrics, everything for value, flow, quality of our work. Where are we on those? Those are reports that we would generate along the way. I wanted to share that.

The other thing that comes in the build phase are decision records. You're also generating architecture decision records. Proposal here is to also generate product decision records as you go along the way. Those then become artifacts. Those are the traces or the pheromones that we leave behind. Then it doesn't matter which agent is there. It doesn't matter if we have cognitive gaps. We can pick it up as we go, depending on the quality of those decisions. Then the other aspect I want to share, this is also coming from past work, not even in the agentic era, but where we were thinking about, strategically, what are all the different ways that we think about providing context to our teams? Going from right to left, so at the organization level, we have our mission and our values and our vision. These don't change as frequently, so there's less volatile.

Then, as you go from right to left, it becomes more volatile. The context is also handed down from right to left. Then information is forwarded from left to right. You'll see goals and outcomes and key results and problem statements and all of that providing the why as well as what are we trying to do, any guidelines about the how we do it, but then also very valuably is how we're going to measure. How we measure, I know right now, I think there were other talks around metrics and stuff too, and it comes up a lot. I wasn't going to go into it too detail in this talk. I think that's a whole other talk and a whole other exploration of what measures are most impactful and don't constrain us and don't become vanity metrics or have unintended consequences, but also thinking about metrics as also evolving.

It's not just a one-time thing but things that would evolve. Here too, if you go right to left, the metrics that are more on the right-hand side may not change as frequently, like KPIs, key performance indicators for your organization don't change as much, because those are ongoing observations. It might be your customer satisfaction. It might also be your code quality, things like that. The key results are things that you're going to do for a particular initiative, for a particular moment in time for a product. Going from the organization to a product to initiative to a task.

How does this apply to agentic coding? The organization here is essentially your agentic team topology, however you may choose to design that. Could be 100 agents working together. It could be five or one. That's something that you would design for yourself, depending on the size of your problem space. I wanted to bring this because I'm not seeing this applied so far as much right now in our conversations because we're talking a lot more about coding. The point is how might we apply things from product engineering there. You'll see here, for instance, the example that we were working with from the life science company. This is just a screenshot coming from basically providing as context to the agent about what we just talked about. Then, actually leveraging the agent to define what is the mission, what are the goals, and so forth. Providing the agent basically the overall structure here and how we want to go about it.

Then you still use the agent to assist you with whatever context you have to accelerate this. Then the agent themselves are creating these documents, these are all Markdown files, for this type of thing. What is going to be the product's KPIs, goals, and so forth? Then you'll see here, it's also developing those decision records, architecture ones, and product decision records. It's part of its now its process as it's working through this canvas that we designed. There's an example decision record around designing a control port for human in the loop. You'll see things like, I've asked it to really think about decay and drift and think about panels, control panels, where I can look at the measures and the metrics and so forth. Then also number five, there is adversarial input. I want to be able to, as a human, actually go ahead and destroy things, remove things, take away things, take away code, or take away a tool that it expected and make sure that it's resilient and recovering.

You'll see some of this output from a dashboard that we had created. It's able to show the decay, the staleness, and so forth. Any drifts that it's able to find. Even adversarial probes, for instance being able to make sure that what we expected, if we do go ahead, and this is talking about patient keys and stuff like that because this is from the life science example I was talking about. You'll see that some of these outcomes are therefore reviewable.

Summary

In summary, some of the takeaways that we talked about. These mental model shifts, consider those. How might they actually enable us evolve our thinking as the industry changes, as we change. Let's not over-constrain ourselves, but at the same time, of course, be responsible with the right bounded context. We talked about a bounded canvas, how you still want to do boundaries but still provide the autonomy so that agents and the generative capabilities of agents can be leveraged. Then, when it comes to stigmergy, leaving traces behind. Whether it's a human agent or a machine agent or whoever changes hands. We're able to also do traceability, be able to understand what it did. In terms of product engineering models, a lot of that work that we did for our own human topologies, how might we leverage that to our machine topologies? Let's think back to it so that the behavioral outcomes are also there, not just the cross-functional ones. Let's design for change and design for failures.

Does this resonate, whether you're a lead architect or a senior leader or a manager or a technologist, this type of way of thinking about bounded autonomy, these are things that we've experienced in many different ways.

Questions and Answers

Participant 1: It definitely resonated with me, a lot of what you had to say. I have two thoughts. One is more of a comment, but it's an insight from a friend. You showed this picture of a dog weighed down by 100 rules. One of the things my friend has been drilling into me is this idea of the model captures all the possibilities that it's been trained on. That when you imagine, like if you were in a situation and someone gave you 100 rules, what kind of response you would have? It's not to be creative and capable. You're asking for a mindless automaton, and that's what you get. A not very skilled junior engineer, where you're treating it like a junior engineer, and that's what you get. If you want a senior engineer, you have to treat it like a senior engineer, and show respect. It just makes sense. Then you're putting yourself more in the probability space of the conversations it's seen with senior engineers where they're very capable, and that's what you're more likely to get out. I thought that was a really interesting way of thinking about it.

One of the things that really has been troubling me is how to keep a view of the architecture as I'm lifting up. You mentioned decision records. I have similar things where it's like, ok, I've got a lot of documents describing things I did and the way I thought about it at the time. The integral of that over time is the architecture, and that is much more challenging to keep up to date, I find.

Nimisha Asthagiri: One of the things maybe I went through is maps. Maps are as critical, I think. Once again, let's take our learnings from architecture and things like that and how it might be applied here. Decision records is very key, and they're too, not all decisions are equal. One of the other guidelines I had provided the agents were also which decisions require human review, which ones don't, which ones require decision records, which ones maybe, so the reversibility of the decisions are there. The other guideline is about drawing maps and keeping those maps up to date. Those maps, we have to be very intentional about which ones matter, and which ones are ok to drift, which ones do we want to keep up to date. By maps there, I'm talking about, it could be the C4 diagrams and the simplicity of that, but don't go all the way down to level 4, not needed anymore. Just level 0, level 1 of C4 diagrams might be sufficient. There might also be maps that sometimes we create from a product standpoint as well. The product strategic maps, lean value tree maps, Wardley mapping, so those things. Just for that context sharing.

Another thing here is that before, people used to put a lot of things in README files, or even in like CLAUDE.md and things like that. The recommendation now is don't, like that's too much, because those CLAUDE.md type files go into the agent's context every single time. It gets too noisy for them. Why do I have to keep hearing that over and over again? It's not applicable for what I need to do now. Really just keep a map of the folder structure. That's enough. Things like that.

One other comment I wanted to make, which I forgot, which is important too, is one of my learnings is also I had all of those strategy docs and all of that. I think I may have overengineered it, because I think there was a little bit of feedback when I was working with the agent about where to start. I do think that's another recommendation here too from the field as well is, don't over-constrain it. You want to be able to build up that. Then over time your harness or your canvas will get better.
